Series::reverse¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::reverse() const -> void
Series::reverse(bool keep_graph,
                bool accumulate_sensitivity = false,
                bool track_higher_order = false) const -> void
Series::reverse(const Series& sensitivity_output) const -> void
Series::reverse(const Series& sensitivity_output,
                bool keep_graph,
                bool accumulate_sensitivity = false,
                bool track_higher_order = false) const -> void

What It Does¶

reverse() launches reverse-mode propagation from the current Series.

If the current Series is the objective, reverse() walks backward through the recorded computation graph and accumulates sensitivities onto tracked input leaves.

This is the Pluss-native reverse-mode entrypoint. In day-to-day code, it is the method you call after the forward computation is complete and you are ready to populate sensitivities on the leaves that had tracking enabled.

Read This First¶

reverse() propagates sensitivity backward from the current output node. The stored result then lives on whichever Series you inspect.

If y was built from x and you call

y.reverse();

then the two most common reads mean different things:

  • x.sensitivity() means dL/dx, which for scalar y is the familiar dy/dx

  • y.sensitivity() means dL/dy, which for scalar y as the objective is usually 1

So the usual workflow is:

  1. mark the leaf or leaves you want tracked

  2. build the forward computation

  3. call reverse() on the finished objective

  4. read sensitivity() from the tracked leaves whose derivatives you want

That rule does not change for products, quotients, chains, trigonometric expressions, or any other composition. reverse() always propagates from the current output back to tracked leaves; sensitivity() always answers “with respect to this specific Series.”

Three nearby methods often get conflated when you first meet this part of the API:

  • tracks_slope_() is the opt-in step. It marks a Series as a leaf that should receive reverse-mode sensitivity later.

  • reverse() is the propagation step. It applies the chain rule from the current output back through the recorded computation.

  • sensitivity() is the read step. It returns the stored sensitivity that reverse() populated on a tracked leaf.

Overload Map¶

There are two independent questions:

  1. Is the current output scalar or non-scalar?

  2. Do you need lifecycle toggles such as graph retention or sensitivity accumulation?

That yields four public shapes:

  • reverse() Use this for a scalar objective when the default one-shot behavior is fine.

  • reverse(keep_graph, accumulate_sensitivity, track_higher_order) Use this for a scalar objective when you need toggle control.

  • reverse(sensitivity_output) Use this for a non-scalar objective, or whenever you want to choose the upstream sensitivity explicitly.

  • reverse(sensitivity_output, keep_graph, accumulate_sensitivity, track_higher_order) Use this when the output is non-scalar and you also need lifecycle control.

Parameters¶

sensitivity_output (const Series&)

The upstream sensitivity to seed at the current output.

This parameter matters whenever the current Series is not scalar.

  • For scalar outputs, you usually omit it and let the method use the implicit scalar seed.

  • For non-scalar outputs, you supply a same-shaped seed that says how much each output position contributes upstream.

That seed is mathematically load-bearing. It defines the weighted scalar objective whose sensitivity will be propagated backward.

keep_graph (bool)

Controls whether the recorded source links used by this reverse pass are kept after the pass finishes.

  • false: one-shot behavior; release what can be released after the pass

  • true: keep the graph links so the same objective can be reversed again

Use true when the same forward result must support multiple reverse passes.

accumulate_sensitivity (bool)

Controls what happens to already stored leaf sensitivities before this pass.

  • false: clear existing stored sensitivities before the pass

  • true: preserve them and add the new contributions on top

This toggle changes result interpretation materially. With accumulation off, each reverse pass gives you a fresh answer. With accumulation on, repeated passes add together.

track_higher_order (bool)

Controls whether the propagation itself should be recorded so higher-order reverse work can be built on top of it.

  • false: ordinary first-order reverse pass

  • true: ask the system to record the propagation path for higher-order use

For ordinary first-order sensitivity extraction, leave this at false.

Returns¶

void reverse() populates sensitivity state on tracked leaves rather than returning a numeric value.

Gradient Model¶

reverse() always computes the sensitivity of a scalar objective with respect to tracked leaves.

That scalar objective can arise in two different ways:

  • directly, because the current Series already has one element

  • indirectly, because you supplied sensitivity_output for a non-scalar result

For a scalar output L, the stored sensitivity on x is the elementwise quantity dL/dx.

For a non-scalar output y, calling y.reverse(sensitivity_output) means Pluss treats the effective scalar objective as

L = sum(sensitivity_output * y)

and then propagates dL/dx backward.

This sum should not be read narrowly as “the only allowed arithmetic total.” It is one standard way of collapsing a non-scalar output into a scalar objective for differentiation. In ordinary user code, any expression whose final result is scalar can play that role: a sum, a weighted sum, a difference, a product, a ratio, or a more elaborate composition.

This is why a non-scalar reverse pass cannot guess its seed. Until you provide that seed, there is no single scalar objective yet.

Examples¶

Example 1. A scalar objective can reverse directly without an explicit seed.

auto x = pluss::make_series(1.25, pluss::cfg::tracks_slope());

auto y = x * x * x - 2.0 * (x * x) + x;
y.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

Here the scalar objective is

L = x³ - 2x² + x

so

dL/dx = 3x² - 4x + 1

Evaluating at x = 1.25 gives

3(1.25)^2 - 4(1.25) + 1 = 0.6875

Output¶

y=0.078125
dL_dx=0.6875

Example 2. A non-scalar result is commonly reduced first, then reversed as a scalar objective.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.mul(pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0}));
y.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

The forward value y is vector-valued:

y = [10x₁, 20x₂, 30x₃]

Here y.sum() is just the chosen scalar objective builder for the example. It is common, but it is not the only possibility.

y.sum() turns this particular vector output into the scalar objective

L = 10x₁ + 20x₂ + 30x₃

Differentiating with respect to x gives

dL/dx = [10, 20, 30]

The actual values of x do not matter here because the objective is linear in each entry.

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[10, 40, 90]
dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[10, 20, 30]

This is the most common pattern for vector-valued forward code: reduce to a scalar objective, then call reverse() with no explicit seed.

Example 3. A non-scalar output can be reversed directly when you provide the upstream sensitivity explicitly.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.mul(x);
y.reverse(pluss::make_series({1.0, 10.0, 100.0}));

std::cout << "y=" << y << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

This is the key seeded case.

The forward output is

y = [x₁², x₂², x₃²]

Because the seed is [1, 10, 100], the effective scalar objective is

L = 1·y₁ + 10·y₂ + 100·y₃
  = 1·x₁² + 10·x₂² + 100·x₃²

Different output positions therefore contribute with different weights.

Now differentiate entrywise at x = [1, 2, 3]:

dL/dx₁ = 1 · 2x₁ = 1 · 2(1) = 2
dL/dx₂ = 10 · 2x₂ = 10 · 2(2) = 40
dL/dx₃ = 100 · 2x₃ = 100 · 2(3) = 600

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 4, 9]
dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 40, 600]

The seed weights the positions differently, so the propagated sensitivity does too.

Example 4. Reversing a non-scalar output without a seed fails explicitly.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.mul(x);
try {
  y.reverse();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Without the seed there is no single scalar objective yet. A vector output has many possible downstream uses, so reverse() cannot guess how those output positions should be combined.

Output¶

series_tape::backpropagate: non-scalar output requires explicit seed

Example 5. With keep_graph=true and the default accumulate_sensitivity=false, repeated reverse passes on the same objective overwrite the stored sensitivity rather than adding to it.

auto x = pluss::make_series(2.0);
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x * x;
y.reverse(true);
std::cout << "first_dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";
y.reverse(true, false);
std::cout << "second_dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

Here L = x², so each reverse pass computes dL/dx = 2x = 4 at x = 2. The only question is whether the second pass replaces the stored value or adds to it.

Output¶

first_dL_dx=4
second_dL_dx=4

Example 6. With accumulate_sensitivity=true, the second pass adds on top of the first one.

auto x = pluss::make_series(2.0);
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x * x;
y.reverse(true);
std::cout << "first_dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";
y.reverse(true, true);
std::cout << "second_dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

The derivative of one pass is still 4. With accumulation enabled, the second pass stores 4 + 4 = 8.

Output¶

first_dL_dx=4
second_dL_dx=8

Examples 5 and 6 are the important toggle pair. The forward objective did not change. Only the accumulation policy changed.

Example 7. An objective with no tracked leaf fails fast. If nothing on the path to x.mul(2.0).sum() was marked for tracking, there is no derivative to propagate, and reverse() raises rather than silently doing nothing.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});

try {
  x.mul(2.0).sum().reverse();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

The scalar objective L = 2x₁ + 2x₂ + 2x₃ is mathematically differentiable, but the graph was never connected: x did not opt in with tracks_slope_(), so the result carries no source link. A reverse pass with nothing to differentiate is a mistake — usually a training loop that would otherwise learn nothing — so it is reported.

Output¶

series_tape::backpropagate: objective does not track slope and has no source link; nothing to differentiate (a constant, or built only from non-differentiable ops)

Example 8. The same failure for a path built only from non-differentiable operations. Here argsort() returns integer positions, which carry no gradient, so even with x tracked the objective is disconnected.

auto x = pluss::make_series({3.0, 1.0, 2.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto ranks = x.argsort(0).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);

try {
  ranks.sum().reverse();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

argsort (and the index channels of sort / topk, argmax, comparisons, integer casts, nonzero(), …) deliberately produce no gradient. A loss built entirely from them cannot be optimized, and reverse() says so instead of returning zeros. Route the loss through a differentiable quantity — sort()’s values, a soft relaxation, and so on — or keep a differentiable term in the objective (see the mixed case below).

Output¶

series_tape::backpropagate: objective does not track slope and has no source link; nothing to differentiate (a constant, or built only from non-differentiable ops)

Example 9. The corrected product-rule usage marks x for tracking before the forward expression is built, then reads the derivative from x.sensitivity().

auto x = pluss::make_series(1.7);
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x * x.cos();
y.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dy_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dy=" << y.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

The forward function is

y = x cos(x)

Use the product rule:

d/dx [x cos(x)] = 1·cos(x) + x·(-sin(x))
                = cos(x) - x sin(x)

Evaluating at x = 1.7 gives

dy/dx = cos(1.7) - 1.7 sin(1.7) = -1.8146746720647213

The output object itself is the scalar objective, so its own stored root sensitivity is 1.

Output¶

y=-0.21903564030239187
dy_dx=-1.8146746720647213
dL_dy=1

Example 10. Quotient-rule objectives work the same way.

auto x = pluss::make_series(1.7);
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.div(x.square().add(1.0));
y.reverse();

std::cout << pluss::series::print(y) << "\n";
std::cout << "dy_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

The forward function is

y = x / (1 + x²)

Differentiate with the quotient rule:

dy/dx = ((1 + x²)·1 - x·2x) / (1 + x²)²
      = (1 - x²) / (1 + x²)²

At x = 1.7:

dy/dx = (1 - 1.7²) / (1 + 1.7²)² = -0.12490004692012345

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=0.43701799485861187
dy_dx=-0.12490004692012345

Example 11. Chain-rule compositions are also recorded correctly.

auto x = pluss::make_series(1.2);
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.square().cos();
y.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dy_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

Here the outer function is cos(u) and the inner function is u = x², so

dy/dx = (-sin(u)) · du/dx
      = -sin(x²) · 2x

At x = 1.2:

dy/dx = -sin(1.2²) · 2(1.2) = -2.3795000356600475

Output¶

y=0.13042370873814554
dy_dx=-2.3795000356600475

Example 12. Scalar objectives do not need to be sums. Any expression whose final result is scalar can be the objective you reverse.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto objective = 2.0 * x.pos(0) + 4.0 * x.pos(1) + x.pos(2).sqrt();
objective.reverse();

std::cout << "L=" << objective.item<double>() << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity()) << "\n";

The scalar objective is

L = 2x₁ + 4x₂ + √x₃

Differentiate entrywise:

dL/dx₁ = 2
dL/dx₂ = 4
dL/dx₃ = 1 / (2√x₃)

At x₃ = 3:

dL/dx₃ = 1 / (2√3) = 0.28867513459481287

Output¶

L=11.732050807568877
Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 4, 0.28867513459481287]

Example 13. Mixed transcendental objectives can combine trigonometric and logarithmic terms, and the stored sensitivity remains the entrywise partial derivative of that scalar objective.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto objective = x.pos(0).sin() - 1.5 * x.pos(1).cos() + x.pos(2).log();
objective.reverse();

std::cout << "L=" << objective.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

The scalar objective is

L = sin(x₁) - 1.5 cos(x₂) + log(x₃)

Differentiate each entry:

dL/dx₁ = cos(x₁)
dL/dx₂ = 1.5 sin(x₂)
dL/dx₃ = 1 / x₃

At x = [1, 2, 3]:

dL/dx = [cos(1), 1.5 sin(2), 1/3]
      = [0.5403023058681398, 1.3639461402385225, 0.3333333333333333]

Output¶

L=2.56430352829672
dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.5403023058681398, 1.3639461402385225, 0.3333333333333333]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • reverse() requires the objective to be connected to the tape. If no leaf on the path opted in with tracks_slope_(), or the path is built only from non-differentiable ops, reverse() raises objective does not track slope and has no source link rather than silently storing nothing.

  • The exact snippet x = make_series(1.7); y = x * x.cos(); y.reverse(); now raises unless you first opt x into tracking; x = make_series(1.7, pluss::cfg::tracks_slope()) (or x.tracks_slope_(true)) fixes it.

  • Reading y.sensitivity() is not the same thing as asking for dy/dx. Read the tracked input leaf you care about, usually x.sensitivity().

  • A loss built purely from non-differentiable results (argsort, sort / topk indices, argmax, comparisons, integer casts, nonzero) cannot be reversed. Keep at least one differentiable term in the objective.

  • Scalar outputs can use the implicit root seed 1. Non-scalar outputs must receive an explicit seed.

  • sensitivity_output changes the mathematics of the result. It is not merely an overload-disambiguation token.

  • keep_graph=true keeps the captured reverse path available for another pass, but it does not by itself request accumulation.

  • accumulate_sensitivity=true adds the new result on top of what was already stored. Leave it false when you want a fresh answer per pass.

  • track_higher_order=true is for higher-order workflows, not ordinary first sensitivities.

Summary¶

Use reverse() when the forward computation is complete and you want reverse-mode sensitivities propagated onto tracked leaves. First decide which leaves should track, then decide whether your output is already scalar or needs an explicit seed, and finally read the result from sensitivity() on the tracked leaves.

  • Series::sensitivity: read the stored result.
